awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation potential of prediction tool to determine physiological pregnancy due date
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is the development of a software tool for personalized pregnancy care. Currently, uncertainty in the ability to predict when labor will begin has significant implications for maternal morbidity and financial consequences for patients and health systems. Consequences range from reduced fetal/newborn survival for preterm to complex prolonged pregnancies, lack of timely access to appropriate levels of care (e.g., rural residents), extended hospitalization for false labor or labor induction, added strain on patients without social support needing to plan work leave or childcare, and higher morbidity and mortality for patients for whom labor is contraindicated. Removing the guesswork around the onset of labor may improve the pregnancy experience and allow women to self-monitor their pregnancies, communicate with their care providers, and access the right level of care at the right time. This technology could provide a tool to monitor physiological change during pregnancy, especially between prenatal care visits, and guide decision-making helping patients as well as care providers across gestation stages. The overall goal is to improve pregnancy outcomes by improving decision-making and addressing uncertainty.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of an artificial intelligence (AI) model to monitor pregnancy and predict when labor will begin. The technology is designed to collect data from a non-invasive wearable sensor to measure skin temperature. An autoencoder was trained using a long short-term memory (AE-LSTM) model on continuously measured temperature data from the skin using a smart ring. Data was used to predict the number of days until the onset of labor. Results show that across 37-42 weeks of gestation, the model predicted the onset of labor 7 days before the participants’ report of symptoms of labor. The research confirmed that the predicted gestation and onset of labor aligned with actual gestational age at labor onset (linear fit of R2 of 0.93). In addition, predictions had an average error of <2 days from the labor onset. The goal is to develop a tool for predicting labor onset that could be employed by pregnant individuals or used by care providers in helping guide care.

por.por_cntn:
In this NSF I-Corps project, our team conducted deep customer discovery to understand the value of a new method for determining how long a pregnancy would be likely to last. Our core technology centers on use of software that can interpret data from wearable sensors and determine how likely it is for a given woman to go into labor in the coming days/weeks.

The outcomes of this project including the training provided by the I-Corps program in developing a business model canvas which helps shape all aspects of the development of the technology into a viable product. We gained insight into the needs of potential end-users of this kind of a technology by conducting >100 interviews of pregnant individuals, care providers (nurses, doctors, midwives) and technology executives in the perinatal or m-health space. Specifically we learned about unique challenges in obtaining timely care in pregnancy across the United States and the desires of pregnant patients to have more high quality access to their care providers. A number of potential partners were identified in this product space as well. 

In the end we developed a customer archetype and several potential channels for go-to-market strategy including B to C and B to B opportunities. We developed a roadmap for next steps in the next phase of this technology that includes several viable strategies, opportunties for funding and scalability.
